analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act's coverage mandates and benefit rules, replaces Medicaid funding with capped block grants, and offers health tax credits and savings accounts.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill died in the Finance Committee with zero cosponsors and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end the Affordable Care Act's requirement that individuals carry insurance and that large employers offer affordable coverage. It would stop requiring insurers to cover a standard set of benefits or provide free preventive care, and would let states let insurers sell skimpy plans with yearly dollar caps on what they pay out. It replaces the ACA's income-based subsidies with a flat tax credit of up to $2,500 per adult and $1,500 per child, but only credits what a person actually spends on premiums or a savings account, and it shrinks what workers with employer coverage get. It would also convert federal Medicaid payments to states into capped block grants and, for most adults, limit federally funded Medicaid to people under the poverty line.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers, which would gain freedom to sell bare-bones plans with annual benefit caps outside the ACA's benefit rules; higher-income households with cash to put into tax-free savings accounts; and employers, freed from the requirement to offer affordable coverage. Some uninsured people would get a new tax credit, but only to the extent they can already pay premiums.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new refundable, advanceable tax credit of up to $2,500 per covered adult and $1,500 per covered child per year, adjustable for age and location, to help pay premiums or fund a savings account.
Creates tax-free 'Roth' health savings accounts that can pay for insurance premiums and medical care, with contributions up to $5,000 a year for individual coverage.
Ends the tax penalty on uninsured individuals and the penalties on large employers that do not offer affordable coverage.
Lets states let insurers sell 'limited benefit' plans with annual dollar caps on payments, and lets a state automatically enroll uninsured residents in a high-deductible plan unless they opt out.
Keeps some ACA protections: no pre-existing-condition denials, guaranteed renewal, dependent coverage to age 26, and no lifetime or annual limits except on the new limited-benefit plans.
Lets states apply a portion of unused tax credits to health care for low-income uninsured residents, and lets Medicaid enrollees opt into private plans with a savings-account contribution.

analysis.who_pays: Sick and low-income people bear the biggest costs: plans no longer have to cover a standard benefit set or preventive care at no charge, and the new credit shrinks for people too poor to spend much on premiums. Medicaid funding becomes a capped block grant, with most adults limited to the poverty line for federally supported care. People going without coverage for a year face a 20% premium surcharge for each year uninsured, and the medical expense deduction is eliminated.

drawbacks.text: Health insurance would no longer be required to cover preventive care at no cost or include the ACA's essential health benefits, so plans could drop maternity, mental health, prescription, and other coverage.
Insurers could sell limited-benefit plans with annual dollar limits on benefits through the exchanges, and those plans are what states must offer to keep the federal tax credits flowing.

Anyone enrolling without 12 months of prior coverage would pay a 20% premium surcharge for each consecutive full year they were uninsured — a penalty that falls hardest on people who could not afford coverage in the first place.
Federal Medicaid payments would become capped block grants, and states could not use federal funds for most adults with incomes above the poverty line, cutting federal support over time.

The new tax credit is limited to what a person actually pays in premiums or savings-account contributions, so someone too poor to buy coverage would receive little or nothing from it, and workers whose employers already cover them effectively lose the credit to the value of the existing employer tax break.

The deduction for out-of-pocket medical expenses would be eliminated, raising taxes for households with large medical bills, such as families caring for a seriously ill member (long-term-care premiums excepted).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's selling point was choice and affordability: no mandates, cheaper skinnier plans, tax credits for everyone. But the design shifts risk onto the people least able to bear it — the credit only pays if you can already spend on premiums, the annual-benefit plans cap what an insurer must pay a seriously ill patient (with a novel provision shielding some of the patient's assets from collection after the cap hits), and Medicaid becomes a capped grant growing without reference to actual costs. The tax advantages run mainly to households with money to save.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2016 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it got no hearing and no vote before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on May 25, 2016; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and no further action was taken for the rest of the 114th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who depend on Medicaid and on ACA coverage protections kept them, because the bill died without a hearing or vote. No interest group is recorded as having pushed for it; it never attracted a single cosponsor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicaid recipients and ACA plan holders

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made no recorded progress on it; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican repeal-and-replace proposal with zero cosponsors and no Democratic support; no roll call was ever taken, so the record shows no bipartisan backing on either side.

industries.note: The bill frees insurers from the essential-health-benefits and free-preventive-care requirements and lets them sell limited-benefit plans with annual payout caps on the exchanges, where the state must offer them to keep federal tax credits flowing. Cheaper bare-bones plans help healthy customers but leave sick patients paying for care those plans refuse to cover.

industries.industry: Higher-income households and financial firms administering savings accounts
industries.note: New Roth health savings accounts let households shelter up to $5,000 a year tax-free for medical costs — a benefit worth most to people with spare cash to save, while the same bill eliminates the medical expense deduction used by families with big bills.

Converting Medicaid to capped block grants and limiting federally funded eligibility for most adults to the poverty line would shrink federal payments over time, including support tied to hospitals that treat large numbers of uninsured patients. Hospitals and their low-income patients lose together.

Repealing the employer mandate and its reporting rules lifts the requirement to offer affordable coverage, saving employers money; the offset is that employees pushed off employer plans would land in a skinnier, deregulated market. Employers could also reimburse individual premiums without triggering coverage rules.
